title: ropeway:handbook-title-52
text: A ropeway is a machine on your mechanical network, like a quern or a helve hammer. The drive turns the haul rope, the haul rope pulls the cabin, and the cabin runs at whatever speed the network is turning. Nothing is stored and nothing is banked: a bigger drive is a faster cabin, and no drive is a cabin that waits. Building the drive 1. Run an axle to any pylon footing on the line. It takes power on either side of the crossarm - the same axis the crossarm runs along, never down the line the cabin travels. 2. Build one tension weight within eight blocks of any tower on the line. It keeps the haul rope taut, and a line will not carry a cabin until it has one. It is not a machine: nothing winds it, it holds no charge and it takes no axle. A bigger mill is a faster cabin Hauling a cabin is a heavy load - about three querns' worth - and the line's speed is what your drive has left over after carrying it. In good wind, on the level: Two sails - a wooden rotor with two sails will not shift the cabin at all. Three sails - about 1.2 blocks a second, a walking pace. Five sails, a maxed wooden rotor - about 2.2. Ten sails, a maxed metal rotor - about 3.0, a run. Where the mill stands matters as much as how big it is Those speeds are good wind, and good wind is the top of the range rather than the middle of it. Wind also strengthens with height. The same maxed wooden rotor that barely creeps the cabin along - a third of a block a second - down at sea level in ordinary weather will run it at over 1.6 from a ridge eighty blocks up, and a three-sail mill in the valley will often not move it at all. Put the drive high. A ropeway is a mountain machine, and so is the mill that drives it. Water wheels A water wheel does not care what the weather is doing, and that is worth a great deal - but it is capped lower than a windmill. Whatever the river does, a water wheel cannot run the cabin past about 1.8 blocks a second, and a sluggish stream will not shift it at all. Constant but capped, against faster but at the mercy of the wind and the altitude: that is the whole choice. Gearing and anything else on a vanilla network behave as they do everywhere else. You never have to guess: a footing's block info panel reads out what the line is turning at and what that comes to in blocks a second. Any tower can take power, and they add up There is no drive station. Put the drive where the terrain suits it - wind on a ridge, water in the valley - and if one mill is not enough, power a second tower somewhere else along the route. Their speeds pool, so two mills is a visibly faster cabin. It has to be a second mill, mind: two footings tapped off the one axle run are the same drive twice over and buy you nothing. Intermediate drive stations were real on long ropeways for exactly this reason: driving the haul loop anywhere along its length drives all of it. Climbing costs A climbing cabin is a heavier load than a level one, so the same mill turns slower while it climbs and picks up again on the flat. On a steep line a small mill crawls. That is the machine working rather than a fault - and it is the honest reason to put a bigger rotor on a mountain line. Dead calm Vanilla weather goes still for hours at a time and no windmill of any size makes torque then. The cabin stops where it is and waits, exactly like a quern with nobody turning it, and sets off again by itself when the wind returns. A stopped cabin is not a locked one - but mind where it stopped. Sneak steps you straight out of it wherever it happens to be, and if that is halfway across a span, you step out into the air and take the fall. Ride it out, or pick your moment. A cabin that is moving refuses that same key press until you hold it down - see Building a Line. If you would rather not wait on the weather, drive the line with something that does not depend on it, or power a second tower somewhere the wind reaches when the first one's does not.
